articles.summary: In "The Angels Among Us," I share a remarkable story about how the blowing of shofar is used by one of God’s angels to bring miraculous healing to journalist Nikki Goldstein.
articles.body: A shofar is made from the horn of a ram and is hollowed out and crafted to be blown like a trumpet. It symbolizes God’s majesty and also serves as a call to repentance. During the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, it is blown as a spiritual wake-up call for us to return to being who God wants us to be. On Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, which ended on Monday night, the shofar is blown at the end of the service to break the day-long fast, with the hope that our prayers have been accepted by God and that we are sealed in the Book of Life for another healthy, prosperous year. The shofar also stands for healing, wholeness, and spiritual redemption. In my new book, "The Angels Among Us," the shofar is used by one of God’s special messengers to bring a miracle recovery to the widely celebrated journalist Nikki Goldstein, in Sydney, Australia. Nikki (57 years old at the time) has had chronic lung disease and an autoimmune disease for many years and has been in and out of the hospital frequently. But in early September 2022, it looks like the end is near. DR MARC SIEGEL: MY PERSONAL MIRACLE: A PHYSICIAN'S LESSONS IN FAITH AND HEALING The CT scan of her chest shows extensive consolidation and scarring, plus a severe acute lung infection. She is put on a ventilator. She is not expected to survive. She says she is giving herself over to God. Her doctor puts her on the emergency lung transplant list. She is put into a coma. Her husband Rowan (who is not Jewish) and her daughter are with her. All at once, Nikki’s daughter looks up and says, "Is that a rabbi?" Nikki’s husband, Rowan, approaches him and says, "My wife would love it if you could say some prayers. This is going to be her last day on earth." The rabbi stands at her bedside and recites prayers for her health. SEARCHING FOR HEROES WITH BENJAMIN HALL PODCAST EPISODE: "CONVERSATIONS WITH MY RABBI" His name, Rowan finds out later, is Rabbi Eli Schlanger, the longtime assistant rabbi at the Chabad synagogue in Bondi Beach. He is portly, with thick spectacles, a bushy beard, and thinning hair. Rabbi Eli is about to leave when he stops and reaches into his jacket and pulls out something shiny. It is his shofar, and he asks if it’s okay to blow it over Nikki. Rowan says, "I cannot think of a single thing she would want more." The rabbi blows the shofar loudly. Twenty-four hours after this, Goldstein’s lungs start to respond. The "whiteout" is improving on her chest X-ray. They wake her up and bring her out of the coma. The whiteout is retreating very rapidly. A medical miracle has occurred. Goldstein goes on to write a book with Rabbi Schlanger, "Conversations With My Rabbi." THE BRAVEST JEWS IN AMERICA ARE 15 YEARS OLD — AND THEY’RE GOING BACK TO SCHOOL It is December 14, 2025, a warm summer's day in Sydney. Near the center of Archer Park, Bondi Beach, in the middle of a celebration (with over 1,000 people attending) for the first night of Hanukkah (the Festival of Lights), right before the menorah lighting, two gunmen open fire in an antisemitic terrorist attack. Rabbi Schlanger sees one of the gunmen pause to reload. Schlanger — the father of five, including a 2-month-old baby — raises his hands above his head and walks toward the terrorists. "Please stop!" he yells. "No more! There has to be another way." One of the gunmen raises his rifle and fires. Schlanger falls to the ground dead. His wife, Chyale, is grazed by a bullet in her back. Their two-month-old baby takes shrapnel to his leg. They survive. He was blowing the shofar when his lips became numb, and he had to stop blowing. "It is a very good thing this happened," he says to her. "Blowing the shofar caused the stroke, but it also caused the doctors to discover that I have diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Blowing the shofar led to the miracle of this life-saving discovery." articles.title: ‘Deadly hazards’: Behind Sudan gold mine collapse, a wartime desperation
articles.summary: Nearly 100 people have died in recent days in the scramble for gold, whose value has grown in a shattered economy.
articles.body:
A gold mine collapse in northern Sudan has killed at least 10 people and injured 21, according to survivors, bringing renewed attention to the dangers facing workers in one of the country’s most important and least regulated industries.

The collapse took place on Sunday at the Awny mining area near Sudan’s border with Egypt. Miners told the AFP news agency they had recovered 10 bodies and pulled 21 injured workers from the site, while the search continued for people believed to be trapped beneath the rubble. It is unclear how many people are trapped in the collapsed mine.

The disaster comes just days after another deadly accident at a gold mine in West Kordofan State. A collapse at the al-Zaraa mine near en-Nahud, a town in central Sudan, left at least 82 people dead.

Sudan is one of Africa’s top gold producers, recording 70 tonnes of production last year, according to the Sudanese government.

Since fighting broke out in April 2023 between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), businesses have been devastated, agriculture has been disrupted, millions of people have been displaced, and Sudan’s formal economy has weakened. In that environment, gold has remained one of the country’s most valuable sources of income.

In July 2025, it was reported by local agencies that Sudan’s gold production rose sharply despite the ongoing conflict, reaching 64 tonnes in 2024, 53 percent higher than the 41.8 tonnes recorded in 2022, and generating $1.57bn in legal export revenues.

However, the gold trade has also become a point of international scrutiny. Most of the gold exports end up in the UAE. In March 2025, Sudan went to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing the UAE of supporting and funding the RSF using gold. The UAE has denied accusations that it supplies weapons to the RSF.

Sudan’s gold deposits are spread across the country, with the majority in the northeast. Port Sudan, the country’s main port, is home to most of the deposits and has been largely controlled by the Sudanese Army since the war began. However, areas controlled by the RSF are also populated by gold deposits.

At the moment, “much of Sudan’s gold is taken out of the country through smuggling or illicit networks instead of passing through government channels that could directly contribute to public revenue,” said Joseph Tucker, senior analyst on the Horn of Africa at the International Crisis Group.

But amid that diplomatic battle and the accusations surrounding gold, the mining deaths in northern Sudan have also raised larger questions over how the country manages the sector, analysts say.

“This disaster is yet another example of the deadly hazards facing those working in Sudan’s gold mines,” Tucker told Al Jazeera. “Most of these (gold mines) are informal, artisanal mines in remote areas that are unregulated and lack modern mining technology, adequate infrastructure, and specialised safety equipment.”

This year, Sudanese Prime Minister Kamil Idris met with the minister of minerals and spoke on the policies for regulating traditional mining and the management and control of various mineral markets. According to French-based Sudanese media, Sudanese authorities called for swift action to address the environmental damage and public health hazards caused by mining activities across the country.

Yet, despite the dangers, Tucker said the state of the Sudanese economy made gold mining appear lucrative to many Sudanese.

During the war, the Sudanese currency’s value has crashed . Before the outbreak of fighting in 2023, about 570 Sudanese pounds could buy a US dollar. By April 2026, the currency had slid to a sixth of that value: It cost 3,500 pounds or more to afford a dollar. That has led to sharp food inflation and a surge in the costs of transport and fuel.

According to estimates by the United Nations Development Programme, Sudan lost $6.4bn of its gross domestic product (GDP) in 2023 alone: That’s a quarter of the country’s $26bn GDP that year. In August, the UN agency reported that 90 percent of the agrarian nation’s farmers had seen yields drop over the previous year.

That economic crisis, Tucker said, “fuels the demand for gold and willingness of miners to work in poor conditions” – even if it proves deadly.

articles.title: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?
articles.summary: An initiative to show that LFW is "bigger than London" launched this year - but will it make a difference?
articles.body:
The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different.

Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world?

The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London".

Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said.

A recent House of Commons report found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022.

However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds.

"A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy.

"But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat.

"I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls.

"Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper."

Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be?

Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle.

She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House.

"London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old.

"You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do."

Bennett says you can harness the power of being different.

"Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says.

Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving.

"The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old.

Natalie Potter is network director at the British Fashion Council, and says the Fashion Britain initiative is "about recognising that British fashion is bigger than London".

Potter says that in the run up to LFW there were events in London, Bristol, Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Dundee and Cardiff.

But what happens after the catwalk leaves town?

Potter says the aim of Fashion Britain is that it will connect talent to "the infrastructure and opportunities that they need to grow".

"So working with the big global businesses that we do across the country to make sure that they've got routes to retail, to give them active mentorship," she explains.

Potter says this will happen "locally and regionally".

This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital.

"I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says.

"There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland".

Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week.

The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry.

"Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion.

"There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says.

For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world.

"Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."

articles.title: A federal judge refused to block a Texas land swap giving SpaceX more than 700 wildlife-refuge acres; the company would surrender 683 acres as opponents continue their legal challenge
articles.summary: US News: A federal judge has refused to block a land swap that would give SpaceX more than 700 acres of a wildlife refuge in Texas. The decision allows the Tru.
articles.body: A federal judge has refused to block a land swap that would give SpaceX more than 700 acres of a wildlife refuge in Texas. The decision allows the Trump administration to move ahead with the exchange while environmental groups and tribal groups continue their legal challenge.US District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr on Monday rejected a request from the groups for a preliminary injunction to stop the exchange. According to news agency Associated Press, the plaintiffs had argued that the deal could increase ecological risks in the Gulf Coast region, which has already been affected by the expansion of SpaceX’s rocket operations.The land being transferred to SpaceX is part of the 103,000-acre Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge. The refuge stretches across four counties along the Texas border and contains animal habitats as well as historical landmarks. The land SpaceX would receive is closer to its launchpad near the US-Mexico border.The US Fish and Wildlife Service approved the land exchange in June. Under the deal, SpaceX would give the federal government 683 acres that it owns in return for more than 700 acres of federal refuge land. The final environmental assessment from the agency said the exchange would have no significant impact on the area and would provide a 'net conservation benefit'.Why environmental groups challenged dealThe land exchange has faced opposition from environmental organisations and tribal groups. The Center for Biological Diversity was among the groups that filed the lawsuit against the exchange. The opponents asked the court to stop the transfer while their broader legal challenge continues.Laiken Jordahl, a spokesperson for the Center for Biological Diversity, described the exchange as a transfer of public land to SpaceX and said it could allow construction activity to move into the refuge. He said the organisation would continue its legal challenge even after the judge refused to issue the preliminary injunction.“This court order is not the final word. These lands hold incredible spiritual, historical and conservation value for the people and wildlife of South Texas. We won’t stop fighting to keep this irreplaceable public wildlife refuge safe from SpaceX bulldozers,” Jordahl said in a statement as quoted by AP.The lawsuit has also raised concerns about the wider impact of SpaceX’s expansion in the area. Opponents have previously criticised the company over its growing footprint, including concerns about access to beaches and rocket launches and explosions.What judge saidRodriguez said the groups challenging the exchange had not provided enough evidence to show that the land would suffer environmental, cultural, historical or aesthetic damage while the lawsuit was still being considered.The judge described the evidence of environmental harm presented by the plaintiffs as “relatively weak”. He also said that although the groups were right to argue that protecting wildlife and historical land serves the public interest, they had not shown that the property would suffer the type of damage required to justify a preliminary injunction.“While they rightfully argue that the preservation of wildlife and historical lands furthers the public interest, they present no evidence demonstrating that the Property will suffer aesthetic, environmental, cultural, or historical degradation during the pendency of this lawsuit,” Rodriguez wrote in his ruling.The judge also considered the possible effect of blocking the exchange on SpaceX. He said an injunction would require changes to the company’s development plans and could create additional difficulties for SpaceX in meeting its milestones and contractual obligations.The ruling, however, does not end the wider legal challenge. According to The Texas Tribune, environmental groups have said they will continue pursuing the case as the land exchange moves forward.What government says The Fish and Wildlife Service's final environmental assessment said the exchange would not cause a significant impact to the area. The agency said acquiring the land from SpaceX would provide long-term conservation value and improve habitat connectivity across wildlife refuges in South Texas.The agency's final assessment covers an exchange of about 715 acres of Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge land for about 683 acres of privately owned SpaceX land. The federal government said the exchange would consolidate refuge holdings and improve the management of protected habitat.SpaceX has expanded its Texas operations rapidly since first breaking ground there more than a decade ago. Its employees voted last year to incorporate their own local government, called Starbase, in the area.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
articles.summary: The UK Foreign Office says it is supporting the man's family and working with local authorities.
articles.body:
Italian authorities are searching for a British man who has gone missing after reportedly diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager.

The man was attempting to rescue two people - a father and son - who were in distress in the water near the San Siro municipality on the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, Italian media report.

The man and the family he was friends with had reportedly been on a boating trip at the time. The father and son were later rescued by another passing boat, but the man has not been seen again.

The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities."

Emergency services - including a helicopter, divers and boat units - have responded at the scene, where the lake's depth can reach more than 200m, according to Italian news agency Ansa.

Rescuers are now preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, local news site Qui Como reports.

The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (11:30 GMT) by the mother of the teenager, who was on a rented boat around 600m from shore with her other child, it said.

The man - who dived in after the father and son after they experienced difficulty swimming and was described as being in his late 30s - began to sink and was not seen resurfacing, the local newspaper reports.

The mother then called emergency services. The father and son were given medical treatment after suffering from the early stages of hypothermia, according to Qui Como.

Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows.

However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward.

articles.title: Dorset Bake Off contestant Danni applied for show 'on a whim'
articles.summary: Danni from Dorset is among the 12 new contestants on the 17th Great British Bake Off series.
articles.body:
A contestant of the new series of the Great British Bake Off has said they applied to take part "on a whim" after getting "sick" of people urging them to apply.

Twelve new bakers will be introduced when the first episode airs on Channel 4 on Tuesday night, including Danni, an HGV service centre administrator from Dorset.

Other contestants include a paediatric doctor, a competitive sprinter, a hairdresser and a drag artist.

Ahead of the first episode, Danni said: "It's going to be so, so fun - I'm definitely watching it. It's going to be so good."

The Bake Off website describes Danni as "naturally curious and experimental" with a love of foraging.

Explaining how they came to be on the show, they said: "It's actually quite a funny story. I applied for the Bake Off on a whim.

"You know when you bring a baked good to any sort of function and they're like 'you should totally go on Bake Off', no matter how good the actual bake is?

"I got sick of people telling me that so I was like 'fine, I'll apply' and then I'll get rejected and then I'll be like 'well, I tried, oh dear'.

Danni, who lives with their parents, sister and three dogs, is also a tech enthusiast and loves decorating bakes with inspiration from video games and animation.

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent's Dorset Breakfast show, they said: "I bake anything and everything. I do love baking so much.

"I'll make sausage rolls one week and the next week it'll be some sort of croquembouche."

When asked about the filming of the series during the hot summer, Danni said: "I won't say how, but the weather certainly did present a challenge.

"But everyone is so nicies all the time and they are so lovely.

"Genuinely, it's such a nice sense of camaraderie in the tent."

The contest, which sees amateur bakers compete to impress celebrity judges with their culinary creations, is now in its 17th series.

Dame Prue Leith, who left the show after nine years, has been replaced by Nigella Lawson.

Previous Dorset contestants have included Maggie from Poole, Carole from Sherborne and Nelly from Christchurch.

articles.title: Trump to speak at United Nations General Assembly
articles.summary: Against a backdrop of global conflicts, the US president is also expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, while an Iranian delegation is in New York. Follow for the latest updates.
articles.body:
• Today at the UN: General debate at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly begins today amid ongoing global crises. US President Donald Trump is the second scheduled speaker of the day, following Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

• On the agenda: Trump is also expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky this morning, after speaking with the leaders of the UK and Japan. He will also take part in a trilateral signing ceremony to formalize a new Greenland security agreement, according to a White House official.

• Main areas of focus: Some of the biggest topics bound to be discussed during UNGA include the war with Iran and wider Middle East instability, the Russia-Ukraine war, climate change and the impacts of AI.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said a new drone agreement is ready to be signed as he arrived in New York for the first day of the United Nations General Assembly, underscoring Kyiv’s push to strengthen its defense capabilities as the war with Russia grinds on.

He did not specify which nations would be involved in the drone deal.

“Ukraine’s number one priority is bringing peace closer and protecting the lives of our people,” Zelensky said, adding that Kyiv would present “concrete security proposals” and de-escalation measures that could “bring the end of the war closer.”

He said Ukraine is also seeking to strengthen its air defenses and secure sufficient financing from partners.

Britain’s newly installed Prime Minister Andy Burnham will hold a high-stakes first meeting with US President Donald Trump today on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

While the two men have spoken on the phone previously, their first face-to-face meeting marks an important diplomatic test for the center-left Burnham, who roundly criticized Trump before he took office. That, combined with Trump’s notorious unpredictability and habit of wading into sensitive political issues like immigration, the prospect of Irish reunification or whether Britain should open new oil and gas fields in the North Sea, makes this a potentially tricky meeting.

Still, Burnham assured reporters Monday that he trusted Trump personally, adding that the “special relationship” between the US and UK remained strong.

“When you come into this job, you realize how deep this relationship is,” he said, according to Britain’s PA News Agency. “We trust our allies. Of course we do.”

Burnham was previously the mayor of Manchester, a city in northern England, and he has tempered his tone towards Trump since becoming prime minister two months ago. He even brushed off Trump belittling his previous job as “the mayor of a town.”

“Now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in,” Burnham said. “And I did say to the president in our first phone call, I said, ‘Mr. President, Manchester isn’t some town,’ I said, ‘This is Manchester.’

“And so yes, the right thing to do is to have a laugh about it, isn’t it, and move beyond it.”

Before the meeting, Downing Street emphasized the defense cooperation between London and Washington, announcing that the UK successfully fired a US torpedo from a British-made undersea drone, the first time either country had fired a torpedo from an uncrewed, underwater vessel.

President Donald Trump will participate in a trilateral signing ceremony with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to formalize a new Greenland security agreement, according to a White House official.

“President Trump will meet with Prime Minister Frederiksen of Denmark and Prime Minister Nielsen of Greenland for a trilateral signing ceremony. The three leaders will formalize their new agreement that will secure and defend the security of Greenland and the United States,” the official told CNN.

The ceremony is the latest update in Trump’s efforts to exert control over the remote island.

Remember : The president floated the idea in January, suggesting that US control in Greenland would be for national security purposes while downplaying the territory’s vast natural resources.

At the time, many Greenlanders expressed opposition to an American takeover of their island, with thousands of demonstrators in Greenland and Denmark protesting against Trump’s calls to annex it.

As Trump repeatedly stated his goal of obtaining Greenland, diplomatic crisis arose within NATO, as the alliance scrambled to defuse the threat.

After a meeting between Danish and Greenlandic officials and Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US, Denmark and Greenland formed a working group to find a “common way forward,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said.

The discourse then largely fell out of public view as the US turned its focus to the war with Iran.

The issue reemerged last Friday as Trump announced that the US reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the US “permanent control” over Greenland’s security and bars adversaries from establishing military bases on the island.

President Donald Trump is scheduled to sit down with Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York today to discuss the next phase of the war with Iran, two US officials told CNN.

Trump last week again insisted that Iran wants to make a deal with the US to end the war.

“Well, hopefully we’re toward the end of the war. They want to make a deal. We’ll see how that works out,” Trump said then about the negotiations process. “Iran is very much wanting to make a deal.”

The president’s comments came after the House voted to approve a measure that would require Trump to end the war. Seven Republicans backed the measure, up from four GOP votes for the last two resolutions on the war.

Axios was first to report the planned meeting with Gulf leaders.

This week, dozens of world leaders are gathering at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, where the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) will take place.

UNGA was established in 1945, the same year that the UN was founded, and is the “chief deliberative, policymaking and representative organ” of the organization, its website says.

The assembly is made up of all 193 United Nations members, who vote on important international issues and take part in high-level debates.

The UNGA also “makes recommendations to States on international issues within its competence,” including political, economic, humanitarian, social and legal matters, it says.

The theme for this year’s general debate at UNGA is “restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all,” according to the UN’s website.

Every year, an UNGA president is elected by the assembly’s members. The post rotates among the UN’s five regional groups: African States, Asia-Pacific States, Eastern European States, Latin American and Caribbean States and Western European and other States.

The president of this year’s UNGA session is Khalilur Rahman, the foreign minister of Bangladesh, whose program is designed around “six interlocking pillars.”

One of these “pillars” involves encouraging the peaceful resolution of conflicts, the protection of civilians, upholding international humanitarian law, and fighting against intolerance, hate speech, and disinformation.

Other “pillars” are focused on topics including sustainability, protecting human rights, digital governance and multilateralism.

World leaders are set to gather in New York to discuss an array of global issues for the annual United Nations General Assembly.

Here’s a look at the state of affairs on some topics that are likely to be mentioned this week:

War in the Middle East: Pauses in hostilities between the US and Iran have not proved lasting , with the sides exchanging on-and-off attacks in the months since they first agreed to a temporary ceasefire in early April. In July, US President Donald Trump said the ceasefire was “over” but negotiations would continue. Traffic remains suppressed in the Strait of Hormuz, hampering the global oil market . Meanwhile, conflicts involving Iranian proxies have raged around the region , and Trump’s Board of Peace has yet to produce a path forward for a lasting end to Israel’s war in Gaza. Trump has claimed many times that Iran is desperate to cut a deal, but has said recently that he expects Tehran to wait until after the November midterm elections because it wants to hurt him politically.

Russia and Ukraine: Years after Russia’s multi-pronged invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the European continent remains roiled by the conflict and a humanitarian disaster is unfolding in Ukraine, which is running critically low on air defenses. Russia continues to hit Kyiv and other cities with drones and missiles, as Ukraine hammers Russian fuel infrastructure. The US sent a high-level delegation to Moscow and Kyiv this month as Washington renews a push to end the conflict, but the visit did not yield any major announcements.

Artificial intelligence: The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on AI on the sidelines of the UNGA Wednesday, sources told CNN. The issue will loom large over the global gathering. Questions about the fast-developing technology have taken on new urgency amid dire warnings about the potential existential threat posed by artificial intelligence. Trump has raged against the idea of government regulation on AI, alleging concerns about the technology are a “hoax ,” though he announced plans last week to create an “AI force” and appoint a US czar to oversee the matter.

President Donald Trump is set to deliver his sixth address to the United Nations General Assembly.

Take a look at key moments from his past speeches to the global gathering:

2017: In his first speech, Trump sought to encapsulate his worldview through the theme of “sovereignty,” suggesting that nations acting in their own self-interest would create a more stable world. He centered the address on reforming UN practices and was optimistic about its ability to improve global security. Trump also brought frank assessments to a range of sticky global flashpoints. He delivered a doomsday warning to North Korea and suggested Kim Jong Un could not survive an American attack. He directed similar ire toward Iran, which he accused of supporting terrorists and destabilizing the Mideast.

2018: Trump’s second address served to reaffirm his commitment to signature policies and convictions. He boasted that his administration “has accomplished more than almost any administration in the history of our country,” which was received with laughter from many attendees. The president also defended his hardline position on Iran and his trade war with China, touted his diplomatic engagement with North Korea, and reaffirmed his rejection of globalism and the prominence of international institutions.

2019: The president spelled out a staunchly nationalistic platform as he opened his third address. Trump slammed China, accusing the nation of breaking promises to the international community to adopt reforms. He took a shot at Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro and also called Iran’s regime one of the “greatest security threats facing peace-loving nations.”

2020: World leaders gathered virtually due to the coronavirus pandemic. Trump praised his own handling of the global health emergency and touted his role in facilitating peace agreements between the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Israel. He attacked China, calling Covid-19 the “China virus” and urging the UN to hold Beijing accountable for the pandemic.

2025: Trump used last year’s address to castigate foreign allies for supposedly ruining their countries with unchecked migration, fueling foreign conflicts with purchases of Russian energy, and ignoring his own peacemaking efforts. He addressed the most pressing foreign conflicts — the wars in Ukraine and Gaza — only in passing, reserving most of his speech to bemoan efforts to combat climate change, tout his administration and take swipes at former President Joe Biden.

CNN’s Kevin Liptak, Jeremy Diamond and Zamira Rahim contributed reporting.

Dozens of world leaders are set to speak at the UN General Assembly this morning, including US President Donald Trump.

Here’s a look at how this morning’s speaking schedule is set to unfold:

Prior to Trump’s remarks to the General Assembly, Secretary-General António Guterres will present his report before the start of general debate.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will then speak first, followed by Trump.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is set to speak later on in the morning, as is Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.

French President Emmanuel Macron will also speak at the assembly, being the 10th of 13 leaders to do so this morning.

Other speakers include the leaders of Jordan, Kyrgyzstan, Lithuania, Peru and Chile. The heads of state from Finland, Luxembourg and Angola are also set to address the assembly in this session.

We’ll keep you across the main headlines from their speeches. Stay with us.

articles.title: Exploring America’s most epic, beautiful (and some say cursed) road trip, along California’s coast
articles.summary: The secret to planning a “perfect” California coast road trip is not to over plan. Be open to discovering treasures along the way and be aware of natural disasters.
articles.body: The notion of taking “the perfect road trip” is one of near legend, but so is the only state you can really have one in. California, by way of the Pacific Coast Highway, is dizzying in its proportions, with the narrow, winding ribbon of road flanked by long beaches and cliffs on one side, and mountains and giant old-growth forest on the other. The landscape is almost too big, too cinematic to process. The nearly 100-year-old route accommodates all budgets and travel interests, an à la carte menu of nature, food, history and recreation. You could have a literary-themed coastal trip as easily as one guided by architecture or birding, surfing, hiking, shopping or wine. But the edge of the nation also courts natural disasters, including mudslides, earthquakes and wildfires. My 300-plus-mile itinerary between Los Angeles and San Francisco dipped in and out of these motifs, with surprises along the way. A road trip along the PCH’s State Route 1 needs planning but also rewards surrendering to serendipity, which is how I unexpectedly began my adventure in Johnny Cash’s bedroom. A Ring of Fire: Casitas Springs to Santa Barbara Some trips end with a pilgrimage site; this trip began with one. In the late 1950s, Johnny and Vivian Cash, his first wife, along with their three daughters, moved from Memphis, Tennessee to California as the fabled singer sniffed out a potential career in Hollywood, like his contemporary Elvis Presley. The Cash family eventually settled more than 70 miles from LA, in the working-class town of Casitas Springs, between Ojai and seaside Ventura. They designed their own version of Graceland, a mid-century-modern ranch house overlooking the valley. “My little piece of heaven,” the Man in Black called it. I learned of the Johnny Cash Mountain Ranch the morning I set out north from LA, from a friend I stopped to visit on my way out of town. A few hours later I was getting a personal tour from the ranch house’s new owner, Lisa Kenton, who bought it with her husband, Jerry. They have since worked to restore the details that match when the Cashes lived there, while also adding memorabilia. As we walked from Johnny’s office to the bedrooms, by way of a sunken living room featuring Vivian’s wagon-wheel chandeliers, Lisa called out, “Alexa, play Johnny Cash.” “Walk the Line” blared as I stepped into the main bedroom. According to a plaque on the house, before it was built Johnny laid down in the dirt and declared, “I want my bed right here.” You can tour the house (the website advertises open days, or larger groups can arrange them), but unlike Graceland you can book a stay in the Cash home, cook on their barbecue deck, swim in their pool and lounge at the poolside bar that was converted from the girls’ playhouse. Hell, you can even write a song there. It only opened to the public two years ago so you might be the first to do that since Cash himself. As I drove north along the PCH and took in the driftwood sculptures erected on surfing beaches, I played my favorite Cash song, “Ring of Fire” (written on nearby Casitas Lake according to Vivian’s autobiography). My next stop was Montecito’s Hot Springs Canyon Trailhead, near Santa Barbara, and its ring of fire of a hike. These natural creek-fed hot springs are among the last in the country accessible and free to anyone — you just need to hike a challenging 1.3 miles into the Los Padres National Forest. Only a few others were at the springs — a cascade of cloudy blue pools as big as hot tubs. As I approached the highest one, a friendly surfer-type in his 60s sized me up as a newcomer and tipped me off that it was the hottest, nearly scalding. A mid-level pool was 7 feet long and a foot deep, the temperature Goldilocks perfect. I soaked until it eased my muscles and boosted my already good mood. I returned to the parking lot just as the sun set and raced to La Playa Azul Café in Santa Barbara for a burrito and margarita before it closed at 8 p.m., scoring a spot on their oasis of a patio. For dessert I walked to the locally famous McConnell’s ice cream on State Street near E. De La Guerra Street, before checking into the Leta Santa Barbara Goleta, an upscale motel with a pool and vinyl shop, owned by Hilton. Water World: Santa Barbara to San Luis Obispo At Santa Barbara Harbor, the outdoor seating area of Dart Coffee lies between the city’s maritime museum and a bright orange, 1960s-era Purisima diving bell. Based on overheard conversations of early-morning customers, many slept the night on their boats. Later, before checking out of my room, I took a cooling dip in the pool. The day’s elemental theme was water. Nojoqui Falls Park is located on a small road off Highway 101 between Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo, but there’s no sign for the turnoff. A short, pleasant trail along a pretty creek takes hikers to the foot of the 80-foot-high craggy waterfall. Due to the dry conditions leading to the coastal fires farther north, the waterfall was far from raging, but it meant I could easily cup it in my hands for a delicious drink. Just beyond the college town of San Luis Obispo, locally referred to as SLO (pronounced “slow”), lies the postcard-perfect state park of Montaña de Oro, where the scent of eucalyptus trees gives way to ocean breezes on the drive to the start of a bluff trail. The park gets its golden name from wild mustard and California poppies that bloom on its hillsides in the spring, but I settled for the bright blue waters and waves crashing against rocks and cliffs. The park’s Spooner’s Cove, named after a family that once resided here, was another gathering spot. A group of teen trail runners cooled down by swimming in the freezing waters beyond its beach. I only allowed my feet to get numb in the small waves. Nearby, in the laid-back twin towns of Los Osos and Baywood, the Sweet Springs Nature Preserve skirts Morro Bay. Other visitors to the preserve included bay turtles, blue herons and a snowy white egret, with kayakers paddling behind them in the bay. The spot is also something of a natural watering hole between the all-porch hangout of Beerwood, and the wood-walled dive bar Niffy’s Merrimaker (locally known as the Marriage Breaker). But the best view was from the rooftop bar at the Hotel San Luis Obispo where I watched the late sunlight dim against the local volcanoes-turned-mountains surrounding the town. Made in California: San Luis Obispo to San Simeon The original Cal Poly university campus there gives San Luis Obispo a youthful energy. The small park in front of the adobe-looking Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa was packed on a Friday night with an all-ages crowd listening to live music. The mission, founded in 1772, is one of 21 in California. The road connecting them (and the towns between San Diego and Monterey) was known as El Camino Real. It was also the setting for the fictional adventures of Zorro, a swashbuckling hero serialized in films and books by Johnston McCulley starting in 1919. Today, El Camino Real is largely Highway 101, running parallel to, and at times overlapping with, Route 1. Other architectural highlights of SLO included a walkthrough of the garish and ornate Madonna Inn, a Disneyland-esque hotel and restaurant. Three miles north on the 101 lies the abandoned sign and main building of the former Milestone Mo-Tel, the first motel in America, which opened in 1925 and closed in 1991. At Cal Poly, there’s a unique park of public architecture structures called the Experimental Practices Laboratory where you hike from one imaginative student legacy project to another, up and down the hills. The most popular sandwich shop in town is, deservedly, the headquarters location of High Street Market and Deli. The Green Bottle bar and beer garden there was a lively spot to hang out in while I waited an hour as they worked through a queue of hungry patrons, for my perfect, stacked garden burger. My next stop was Cayucos, another popular beach town with a pier, this one with a view of the iconic Morro Rock, likewise jutting into the ocean. I scored a stool at the popular upstairs bar at Schooners where sea breezes rolled in through the open windows. Then it was on to the towns of Cambria and San Simeon, where I began retracing my steps from Cali road trips past, which largely demonstrated how little has changed in the area over the last 25 years. The Piedras Blancas Elephant Seal Rookery (7 miles north of San Simeon) remains full of massive, delightfully noisy beasts. They’re protected from sharks by all the kelp growth in that spot, explained a volunteer docent who also shared that the beach’s live cam gets rather steamy in January. Twenty-five years earlier I’d also visited San Simeon’s Hearst Castle, bespoke home of media mogul William Randolph Hearst, now more famous for his fictionalized portrayal in Orson Wells’ “Citizen Kane.” It’s a stunningly beautiful, if ostentatious, display of architecture, especially in contrast to an otherwise undeveloped region of the coast — yet I was surprised to see the parking lot packed. Sure, Hearst was once Elon Musk-famous, but he died 75 years ago. Luckily for all the visitors, the castle was later donated to the state to keep its legacy intact. The farthest north I’d reach that day was the stunning 150-foot-high Ragged Point, 15 miles beyond San Simeon. A challenging trail takes you to a mashup of rocks and waves at the bottom. At the top, next to the Ragged Point Inn, stands a wooden ring sculpture called “Portal to Big Sur,” and through it you can see miles ahead — miles that would remain inaccessible during this trip. Just a mile or so north of Ragged Point on Route 1 a closed road sign and police car behind it turned me around. Two uncontained wildfires near the coast had been causing evacuations and business closings in the weeks and days ahead of my visit. Only a few days earlier, I received a call canceling my yurt reservation at the Big Sur glamping spot Treebones. Instead, I doubled back to the San Simeon Lodge motel. It was clean and comfortable but no Hearst Castle or even Treebones yurt. Into the Fire: Cambria to Big Sur Due to the closing of 30 or so miles of the PCH, I had to drive south and connect with the 101 north in order to go around the fires, and back out to the coast and down to Big Sur that day. It was a 190-mile backwards ‘C’-shaped detour. My personal ring of fire. But first, I parked in the middle of Cambria, a charming strip of a town, for olallieberry pie for breakfast. Linn’s, decorated with vintage bikes mounted along its high walls, lived up to the hype. My slice was an alchemy of crust and rich berry, somewhere in the blue to blackberry spectrum. Linn’s also uses it for cream puffs, muffins, milkshakes and tea, but “pie is our why” read my coffee mug with their slogan on it. On my detour along the 101 I took in the mountains in the distance and farmland in between. Workers were picking the rows of vegetables or wine grapes, recalling John Steinbeck’s “The Grapes of Wrath,” one of two books I reread for this California adventure. I was, as Steinbeck wrote in it, “going to California really to go home again,” meaning it was one of those destinations you visited for the purpose of going back home to tell people about. Bragging. Once I circled back to the coast I decided to give Monterey, and later Santa Cruz, the short shrift. While they have their histories, charms and attractions (a world-class aquarium in the former, and vampires in the latter, according to the 1987 film “The Lost Boys”), I prioritized small towns and big nature instead. Of all the beautiful hikes I enjoyed on this trip, the most breathtaking was in Point Lobos State Natural Reserve, less than 4 miles south of the boutique-y Carmel-by-the-Sea, where Clint Eastwood was once mayor. The eponymous trees of the Cypress Grove Trail framed pelicans flying in formation at eye level, above clear turquoise ocean waters crashing against jagged sea walls. Everyone I heard, as they rounded the trail to the northern tip, uttered a variation of “Oooh!” or “Wow!” It was another sunny day with no visible smoke, but smaller roads and state parks were closed for emergency vehicles. Handmade signs thanked the firefighters as I entered the Big Sur region. Just after crossing the oft-photographed Bixby Bridge, a California Highway Patrol officer was writing out tickets to those parking unsafely at the edge of Route 1 to snap their selfies with the nearly 100-year-old crossing. Having reread Jack Kerouac’s “Big Sur” just before my trip I was disappointed that, because of wildfire threats, I couldn’t take the narrow Coast Road into Bixby Canyon (called Raton Canyon in the book). I’d wanted to find the spot where the writer stayed and wrote about, a cabin belonging to his friend, poet Lawrence Ferlinghetti. It was in “Big Sur,” published in 1962, that I first heard of the legendary Nepenthe restaurant, the most famous in that area of the coast. Sixty-four years later it’s still “a beautiful clifftop restaurant with vast outdoor patio, with excellent food, excellent waiters and management, good drinks, chess tables, chairs and tables to just sit in the sun and look at the grand coast,” as Kerouac reviewed it in his book. He took some creative license by calling their signature sandwich, Ambrosia burgers, “Heavenburgers.” Nepenthe comes from the Greek meaning “no sorrow” and was an ancient Egyptian drug to induce forgetfulness, according to the menu. My sorrowless meal was enjoyed outside on the deck, 808 feet above the ocean, at sunset, on Labor Day. My server said most years that holiday is their busiest, with a 3-hour wait (they don’t take reservations). But I wasn’t lucky, I was tenacious. With a lot of Big Sur shut down and inaccessible from the south, and only days from the end of a mandatory evacuation, many visitors assumed the place was closed — even though Nepenthe kept its website updated throughout. I had the vegetarian version of the Ambrosia burger and a light and refreshing local Albariño wine by La Marea, from an extensive list of options. Just after the sun melted into the sea a deer trotted by, followed by its more nervous baby. The redwood interior of Nepenthe is beautiful as well, a large round fireplace and the bar balance each other out. That night I stayed at the historic Deetjen’s Big Sur Inn, less than a mile from Nepenthe. But before I tucked in, I strapped on a headlamp and hiked up the road behind the Inn, along a little creek and multi-story redwoods. The road twisted back for an expansive view of the coast and more stars than I’ve seen since I don’t know when. Milky Way dense. Discernible satellites. A bright Venus outshining everything. And the only sounds were crickets and waves crashing far below. Another perfect moment. Into the Sunset: Big Sur to Pescadero Deetjen’s Big Sur Inn is historically rustic. The rooms don’t have keys. Cell service, much less Wi-Fi, is not available. One of its old-world charms is the handwritten guestbooks (they call them journals) in each room. I stayed up reading mine, in Little Room. It was packed with tiny biographies, poetry, words of gratitude and drawings (especially of the sweet resident cats). One little kid used several pages to start an illustrated novel. They came for honeymoons, anniversaries, birthdays or just escapes from the real world (aided by lack of internet). Deetjen’s is on the National Register of Historic Places, one of the few spots that catered to early travelers on the old Carmel-San Simeon Highway, the first stretch of what would become Route 1. I slept deeply in a darkness and quiet rarely found in any accommodation today. Even if you don’t stay at the inn, try to book dinner or breakfast at its restaurant, which was originally built as a barn in the late 1930s by Norwegian Helmuth Deetjen himself, from local redwoods and materials reclaimed from Monterey’s famous Cannery Row (immortalized by another Steinbeck novel). Visibility driving back north was hazy with wildfire smoke that morning. I had to skip the Henry Miller Memorial Library cabin and Andrew Molera State Park, where the river meets the ocean — both closed. By the time I reached Monterey it was blue skies again. And I was making fast time because Route 1 temporarily turns into a highway until Santa Cruz. Just shy of the fun college town of Santa Cruz, I stopped for a fancy lunch at the Shadowbrook Restaurant in Capitola. The small beach town has brightly painted houses, an old train bridge, a river with homes and little shops along it. Shadowbrook’s website says “it’s not about the cable car” that you can take down to their riverside patio, but it kinda is. The Pacific Coast Highway narrowed to two lanes again and the coast resembled the giant sandcastle cliffs of Limbo, as depicted in Christopher Nolan’s “Inception.” I was in a hurry — rare for this trip — to check into my final accommodation: a hostel located on the grounds of a historic lighthouse in Pescadero called Pigeon Point. The 115-foot lighthouse was built in 1872 to keep travelers safe between Monterey and San Francisco before there was a PCH. The lighthouse itself is being restored but it has a small museum, gift shop and a hostel where you can book a private room or, for only $40 as I did, a bed in a shared room. Everyone has use of a common kitchen and living room, and Wi-Fi. Although my room had six bunks, my only roommate was a quiet man from Switzerland who was also traveling from LA to San Francisco, but by bike. He too had to make a wide detour around the fires. I was eager to check in at the earliest time because that’s also when you can book the private, outdoor, cliffside hot tub (30 minutes for $10). I knew exactly when I wanted it. Over dinner at the nearby Cascade Restaurant, I thought of how far I’d come and how it seemed much longer than what you can reach on two tanks of gas. Traveling the liminal space between the state’s most famous cities felt like I’d circumnavigated a small country. Back at the lighthouse and only minutes before sunset, I walked out on their small deck containing little more than a hot tub and 180-degree view of cliffs and ocean. As a formation of pelicans flew by only feet away and waves danced below, I sank down just as the sun did on the red-yellow horizon, a beautifully epic ending to what felt like the perfect-as-it-gets coastal California road trip of my dreams.

articles.summary: A key text message from UVU's police chief could help Charlie Kirk's family pierce Utah's governmental immunity shield in their wrongful death claim.
articles.body: Utah law granting broad immunity to government entities and their employees could make it difficult for Charlie Kirk’s family to pursue a wrongful death claim against the state and Utah Valley University — but there's a key piece of evidence they've raised in legal filings that could clear the hurdle, according to a trial attorney and legal analyst. "Utah law makes it very difficult for the Charlie Kirk family to proceed with a civil claim against the state and the university," said Randolph Rice, a Maryland-based attorney and former prosecutor who is following the case. A judge dismissed the case on governmental immunity grounds. The Petito family is appealing. Kirk's family filed a notice of claim, which is a precursor to a lawsuit, last week — alleging that Utah Valley University, the state of Utah and key officials failed to properly secure the event even after acknowledging responsibility for rooftop security, leading to his wrongful death. articles.title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular accused of rape, drugging in Massachusetts
articles.summary: US News: Online streamer Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular, faces two felony charges in Massachusetts — rape and drugging a person for sexual intercour.
articles.body: Online streamer Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular, faces two felony charges in Massachusetts — rape and drugging a person for sexual intercourse — and a liquor-related misdemeanor involving a person under 21. His arraignment is scheduled for October 14.The case was filed on September 8 over alleged offences on May 23, 2025. The publicly available docket gives no further account of the conduct underlying the charges.The rape count falls under Chapter 265, Section 22(b) of Massachusetts law and carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in state prison for a first offence. A separate felony count under Chapter 272, Section 3 concerns drugging a person for sexual intercourse and carries a sentence ranging from 10 years to life imprisonment upon conviction.A conviction on either felony count would fall within Massachusetts law's definition of a sex offence for registration purposes. The charges are allegations and do not establish guilt.Peters has gained an online following around “looksmaxxing”, an internet trend centred on attempts to maximise physical attractiveness, including through extreme appearance-altering practices.Separate Florida lawsuit alleges sexual misconductThe Massachusetts prosecution follows a separate civil lawsuit filed against Peters in Florida earlier this year. The lawsuit alleges battery, fraud, intentional infliction of emotional distress and unauthorised use of name and likeness.The plaintiff alleged non-consensual sexual encounters with Peters at his family's Cape Cod home while she was intoxicated. The complaint also alleged that Peters injected her face with Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving substance, without her consent during a livestream, reported by CBS Miami.The lawsuit describes alleged incidents beginning in 2025. Peters later responded on social media by saying women were seeking money from him.His lawyer in the civil case rejected the allegations and said Peters would contest the claims.Representative says Peters not served with warrantPeters' representative Mitchell Jackson said no arrest warrant had been served on him. “Braden Peters has not been physically served,” he said, while accusing The Bulwark, which first reported the charges, of exaggerating the status of the case, reported by NBC News.No defence lawyer was identified for Peters in the online criminal docket at the time of the report. It remains unclear from the criminal docket whether the Massachusetts prosecution stems from conduct described in the Florida lawsuit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Autumnal equinox marks start of fall, but heat could stick around
articles.summary: Fall officially starts on Sept. 22, but the temperatures still may be warmer than expected.
articles.body:
Our long, hot summer is finally coming to an end this evening with the autumnal equinox, which marks the beginning of fall here in the Northern Hemisphere.

At a precise moment each September, usually on the 22nd or 23rd, the sun is directly above the equator, marking the autumnal equinox in the Northern Hemisphere.

(South of the equator in the Southern Hemisphere, it's known as the vernal or spring equinox and marks the beginning of spring.)

But what weather will the U.S. see this fall, given the record hot August and a forecast that calls for El Niño to peak either in late fall or early winter?

Read on for the forecast and also a look back at some of the statistics that made the three-month summer so remarkable.

Best leaf-peeping destinations in the US, according to Priceline

The transition into fall brings the opportunity for scenic leaf-peeping trips. Some domestic destinations come alive as the seasons change, with foliage turning vibrant shades of orange, amber and red. Here are this year's hottest leaf-peeping destinations in the U.S., according to Priceline booking data for October 2026 trips. Topping the list is the Adirondacks Region in New York. Its leaf-peeping season is one of the longest in the nation, with the mountain range coated in color, and visitors can partake in autumn festivities like Oktoberfest.

The exact time of the equinox is 8:05 p.m. ET. The equinox occurs at the same moment worldwide.

The word equinox comes from the Latin words "aequalis" and "nox," meaning equal night. On the autumnal (and the spring) equinox, day and night are both roughly 12 hours long in most of the world.

This will be true Sept. 22 from as far north as Utqiagvik (formerly Barrow), Alaska – north of the Arctic Circle – to as far south as Wellington, New Zealand, the world's southernmost capital city.

Day and night aren't exactly 12 hours long on the day of the equinox because the Earth's atmosphere refracts, or bends, light in an optical illusion that brings more daylight than there really is. Because of this, the date when day and night are of equal length is usually a few days after the autumnal equinox.

Astronomical fall vs. meteorological fall

Although some people say the autumnal equinox is the "official" start of fall, no administrative or political organization actually designates that.

In fact, though astronomers say summer ends Sept. 22, meteorologists and climatologists say summer ended Aug. 31, the final day of the three hottest months of the year (June, July and August).

Cooler temperatures? Maybe, but warmer than normal

If you were looking forward to cooler temperatures this fall , you might be disappointed. Thanks to a combination of El Niño and climate change , there's a high likelihood for warmer than normal temperatures to continue this fall, said Zach Labe, climate scientist at Climate Central.

" The summer that is just ending was one for the record books, with record ocean heat, the warmest month recorded globally," Labe said. "And extremes like these could be just the beginning."

Worldwide, August was the warmest on record for land and ocean temperatures combined and the August average in the U.S. set records in terms of maximum, average and minimum temperatures, Labe said.

"El Niño is all about redistributing heat," so the heat comes from the ocean and is transferred into the atmosphere, Labe said. That's why El Niño years often add an additional boost to global temperatures.

Through August, the average temperature in 2026 has been the warmest on record in the contiguous United States, and Arizona, California, Colorado, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah and Wyoming each had their warmest start to the calendar year on record, he said.

Even though we're likely to hear more and more about warm temperature records being broken, "it's not really El Niño that is breaking those records," Labe said. "It's human-caused climate change. That's what's driving the long-term trend."

Federal forecasters expect El Niño to peak later this fall and to be one of the strongest El Niño events on record, "but that doesn't always necessarily mean stronger impacts, " Labe said. "Every El Niño has its own flavor. Each one is different. And so that's really important to keep in mind."

articles.title: Australia confirms F-35 fighter jet parts were mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong
articles.summary: Australia’s defense minister said Tuesday that F-35 fighter jet parts had been mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong, following reports US lawmakers were investigating the mishap amid concerns about the possibility of China getting access to sensitive US military technology.
articles.body: Australia’s defense minister said Tuesday that F-35 fighter jet parts had been mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong, following reports US lawmakers were investigating the mishap amid concerns about the possibility of China getting access to sensitive US military technology. “We’ve been made aware of this, and we’re obviously working with the United States and Lockheed in terms of how we can assist in this investigation,” Defense Minister Richard Marles told reporters in Adelaide. Politico first reported last week that the F-35 parts shipment bound for the United States for repairs were rerouted in transit from Australia this summer, citing three people familiar with the matter. An intermediary was transporting the parts on behalf of F-35 manufacturer Lockheed Martin, the outlet reported. It wasn’t immediately clear why the shipment was rerouted or how it ended up in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China. US officials have long been concerned about China’s ability to obtain sensitive information on advanced American weapons, including F-35 design information. A US Air Force report in June detailed how Beijing has closely watched US progress, trying to replicate its advantages while scaling up development in stealth aircraft and anti-stealth air defenses, as China seeks to aggressively expand its military power. According to the Politico report, the incident has sparked a series of briefings for congressional staff on key national security committees as it investigates the diversion. State Department and Pentagon officials briefed congressional staff in June, with multiple additional briefings expected in the coming weeks, it reported. On Tuesday, the Pentagon confirmed the disappearance of some components, with a Department of Defense spokesperson telling CNN that Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Program Office was “aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components.” The fifth-generation F-35 Lightning II is largely seen as the world’s most advanced fighter jet, with Lockheed billing it as the “most lethal, survivable and connected fighter aircraft.” “We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the Defense Department spokesperson told CNN. Marles said Tuesday it was his understanding that no sensitive parts were in the missing shipment. “We are examining very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end, but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program,” Marles said. “This is ultimately a matter for the US and Lockheed, as its prime contractor and the contractor that is responsible for managing the global supply chain,” he added. CNN has reached out to the Australian Defence Force for more detail. In a statement to CNN, Lockheed said it couldn’t discuss the status of shipments for security reasons but said it follows regulations set by the US Defense Department and the Defense Logistics Agency. “Our teams handle every shipment with the utmost diligence and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 program and the security of our allied partners,” Lockheed said. CNN has reached out to the State Department and the US House and Senate Armed Services committees. The Hong Kong government declined to comment to CNN. The US consulate in Hong Kong directed CNN to the State Department. Only eight countries have F-35 programs: the US, UK, Australia, Italy, Netherlands, Canada, Denmark and Norway, according to Lockheed’s website. Australia received its first F-35 in 2014, with its Air Force reaching full operational capability in 2025, the website said. This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: From the Chargers to the Colts and Falcons, which of the NFL's eight winless teams are already in panic mode
articles.summary: Eight NFL teams, including the Colts and Chargers, sit at 0-2, and history says only one of the eight will probably make the postseason so who's panicking
articles.body: We are only two games into the NFL season and already multiple teams need to be in full-on panic alert. That's because the season offers only 17 games and losing the first two is, well, a major problem. Forty teams have started a season 0-2 since 2021 when the league went to a 17-game schedule. Of those 40 teams, only eight rallied to make the playoffs. That means 20% of the teams starting 0-2 since 2021 made the postseason. And 80% did not. COMMANDERS FACE CRITICAL DECISION ON JAYDEN DANIELS' ELBOW AS SPECIALISTS REVIEW MRI RESULTS If the math holds, that means maybe only one of the eight teams that started the season with a 0-2 record will make it to the postseason. So, yeah, fanbases are panicking. Pundits invested in their opinions looking good are panicking. And teams are trying to resist the urge to panic. But which of the NFL's eight winless teams legitimately should panic? Here are the answers: Los Angeles Chargers: Definitely time to panic. John Harbaugh has never been 0-2 in his life and there is nothing that suggests he knows how to handle the crisis. He handed the reins of the offense to new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who is busy ruining quarterback Justin Herbert. McDaniel flipped Herbert's shotgun stance, gave him an offense built to have Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle but lacks both, and isn't known for making adjustments. Oh, yeah, check out the killer schedule for the next seven games. Houston Texans: Not time to panic yet because this team under coach DeMeco Ryans has been a notoriously slow starter. They started 0-2 in 2023 and again last season, and made the playoffs both seasons. But this year they've lost two home games to open the season, and another loss will have fans and media in Houston losing their minds. The offensive line is a problem, there is no dynamic playmaker at running back, and the defense which finished second in points allowed last season is currently ranked 25th. Indianapolis Colts: Head coach Shane Steichen and general manager Chris Ballard must win or they'll be fired. Problem is, the Colts have lost nine consecutive games dating back to last season. Cornerback Sauce Gardner, who joined the team last November in a blockbuster trade that sent two first-round picks and a player to the New York Jets, has not won a game with the Colts in the United States. Another loss Sunday, coincidentally against the Texans, will make this a serious panic situation because jobs are at stake. Miami Dolphins: No panic here. The Dolphins are a borderline Triple-A team and ownership, the personnel department and the coaching staff pretty much knew this before the season because that's how they authored it. It's one reason coach Jeff Hafley actually said, "success is not gonna be measured in wins and losses." The Dolphins are on a March to Arch (Manning) and they're right on course. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Tennessee Titans: It's not correct to say they're panicking because it's a first-year coaching staff and quarterback Cam Ward is only in his second NFL season. But owner Amy Adams Strunk in recent years has not blinked at getting rid of a couple of highly touted QBs while they were still on their rookie contracts, and a coach who lasted less than two seasons. This is not a stable or patient franchise, so panic is not far off barring a change of direction. Washington Commanders: This is a desperate team. They have not only lost games but lost starting quarterback Jayden Daniels to a dislocated elbow. He may need surgery, which would end his season and effectively dash the team's postseason hopes. The Commanders badly need good news on the Daniels front because panic is this close to setting in. BAKER MAYFIELD LOSES BET TO COACH TODD BOWLES, HAS 'ROUGH COUPLE OF DAYS' INCLUDING AT PRESS CONFERENCE Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Todd Bowles wouldn't have panicked if he'd woken up in a flooded stateroom on the Titanic. But quarterback Baker Mayfield isn't wired like that. He's passionate, sensitive, and often led by raw emotion. So the danger of panic is real for a player pressing after getting a big contract and, so far, not living up to the bigger bucks. Atlanta Falcons: They're not panicking yet because Michael Penix Jr. will start his first game of the season on Thursday. Any team getting its presumptive starting quarterback back in the lineup for the first time is actually upbeat rather than panicking. But Penix Jr. better perform, and the results must change. articles.title: Charges against pro-Palestinian Stanford protesters to be dismissed
articles.summary: Charges against five ​former and current Stanford University students will be dismissed in relation to ‌a 2024 pro-Palestinian demonstration in which protesters barricaded themselves inside the school president’s office.
articles.body: Charges against five ​former and current Stanford University students will be dismissed in relation to ‌a 2024 pro-Palestinian demonstration in which protesters barricaded themselves inside the school president’s office. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said Monday it would dismiss the charges if the five defendants completed 100 hours of community ​service each and paid about $52,000 combined in restitution to the university. Santa Clara County ​Deputy Public Defender Avi Singh, who represented one of the defendants, ⁠said all had “made full restitution and agreed to complete substantial community service so they ​can move forward with their lives,” according to the San Francisco Chronicle. A judge declared a ​mistrial in February in the case after jurors could not reach a verdict. Twelve protesters were initially charged with felony vandalism. Seven of them previously accepted plea deals or diversion programs. Prosecutors said at ​the time the charges were filed that at least one suspect entered the building ​by breaking a window. Police arrested 13 people on June 5, 2024, in relation to the incident ‌and ⁠the university said the building sustained “extensive” damage. The charges were among the most serious against participants in the 2024 pro-Palestinian protest movement on U.S. colleges in which demonstrators demanded an end to Israeli attacks and strikes on Gaza and to Washington’s support for its ally, ​along with a divestment ​of funds by ⁠their universities from companies supporting Israel. Protesters had renamed the building “Dr. Adnan’s Office” after Adnan Al-Bursh, a Palestinian doctor who died in an Israeli ​prison after months of detention. Over 3,000 people were arrested during ​the 2024 ⁠U.S. pro-Palestinian protest movement, according to media tallies. Some students faced suspension, expulsion and the revocation of their degrees. After the mistrial, Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen said he would seek a ⁠new ​trial. However, defense attorneys were able to successfully argue ​that his office should be removed from the case, citing concerns including his past remarks. The California attorney ​general’s office took over the case.

articles.title: Man challenging 150-year-old ban on making liquor at home hopes Supreme Court takes his case
articles.summary: An Ohio man's Supreme Court case challenges a more than 150-year federal ban on home distilling that carries felony charges, fines and up to five years in prison.
articles.body: Americans can brew beer in their kitchens and make wine at home, but just try making a bottle of whiskey or gin — and people can run afoul of a federal law that dates back more than 150 years. That distinction caught the attention of Ohio resident John Ream, a former aerospace engineer and home-brewing enthusiast who wants to distill small quantities of spirits at home for himself and his wife. "It is perfectly legal to make beer at home or to make wine at home, but if you make even a single ounce of distilled spirits at home, it is a federal felony," Robert Alt, an attorney representing Ream, told Fox News Digital. GEORGE WASHINGTON'S 1757 BEER RECIPE BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE AHEAD OF AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY Ream's interest in making his own drinks began when his then-fiancée, now wife, Kristin, gave him a home-brewing kit. "Brewing was the perfect combination of art and science, and my engineering brain just totally latched onto it," Ream told the Buckeye Institute, an Ohio-based think tank where Alt serves as president and CEO. After years of experimenting with brewing, Ream and his wife opened Trek Brewing Company in Newark, Ohio. But when Ream became interested in experimenting with distilled spirits at home, he encountered a very different set of rules. 'GOD BLESS THE USA' STAR REVIVES PATRIOTIC SPIRIT BRAND BENEFITING VETERANS FOR AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY Federal law allows qualifying home production of beer and wine for personal or family use — but distilled spirits cannot legally be produced at home. Federal violations can carry significant fines and prison time. The debate has also attracted attention within the home-brewing community. "This would be a wonderful opportunity to raise a glass to freedom and to limited government." The American Homebrewers Association, a trade group based in Boulder, Colorado, said this year that it does not have an official position on legalizing home distilling. It noted that some of its members distill at home and emphasized education and safety around beverage-making hobbies. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Why federal law treats distilled spirits differently from beer and wine has roots stretching back more than two centuries. The federal government began taxing distilled spirits in 1791, a levy that helped spark the Whiskey Rebellion several years later, according to the National Archives. In 1868, amid concerns about tax evasion and the collection of liquor taxes, Congress enacted a broader system regulating distilled spirits that included restrictions on where distilleries could operate. More than 150 years later, that old tax fight has produced a modern question. "To what extent can Congress regulate local non-commercial otherwise lawful [activity] that you engage in, in your very home?" Alt said. "That really is the core question in this case." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Two federal appeals courts have given different answers to the constitutional question behind that debate. The Sixth Circuit ruled against Ream in April, concluding that the home-distilling restriction could lawfully be used to support the collection of federal liquor taxes. But 11 days earlier, the Fifth Circuit reached the opposite conclusion in a separate challenge, ruling that Congress' taxing authority did not justify the restriction. Both disputes have reached the Supreme Court, though the justices have not agreed to hear either case. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The Supreme Court gets a lot of petitions for review every year, between 7,000 and 10,000," Alt said. "And the court, at this point, only hears about 60 cases." The federal government argues that the restriction remains a permissible part of the system used to protect and collect federal excise taxes on distilled spirits. Ream and other home-distilling advocates contend that collecting those taxes does not give Congress the authority to prohibit the hobby altogether.
